<reason>Both sides were strong, but B built the cleaner path under the motion's wording. B's counterfactual framing — the real alternative is a vacancy-ridden five-day week, not an ideal one — survived the whole debate, and A effectively conceded it in Rebuttal 2 ("the honest five-day comparison has a vacancy"). A's signature dilemma ("money or hours, not both") collapsed when B showed, using A's own concession, that savings live in fifth-day operating lines untouched by longer weekdays; A's retreat to "a sliver" was then met with the decisive symmetry point that rural deficits are the same size as that sliver. B also left two live mechanisms unanswered by A: the compounding vacancy (algebra→geometry→precalculus) and attendance. A landed real hits — retention's invisibility in achievement, popularity-not-learning, the asymmetry of a zero ceiling — but B's "retention is the help the motion names regardless" and "near-zero harm cannot outweigh positive savings and retention" answers anchored the weighing. A's case increasingly rested on an asserted prediction that adopters will compress hours, which B contested with hour-preserving evidence and legal minimums. Both used Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 formats properly; clips were minor and roughly even. No fake sourcing on either side.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's dismantling of A's "money or hours, not both" trap: B2.1/B3-Q1 used A's own A1.4 concession (savings come from buses, food, utilities, not teacher hours) to show the savings survive full hour preservation, and A's A4.1 retreat to "the savings exist but are capped at a sliver" confirmed the collapse — which B4 then compounded with "small budgets make small lines decisive." Runner-up: B's compounding-vacancy mechanism ("zero compounded over twelve years is zero; a year of substitute algebra compounds into no precalculus"), flagged as unanswered in B2.5 and never addressed again.</best_rebuttal>
